### ILO 169 convention and its implications in Chile _page 2_ 

In April 2012, the Supreme Court of Chile upheld a February ruling by the Court of Appeals of Antofagasta to suspend the approval of the EIS for the El Morro copper-gold project. The reason given was the lack of compliance with the ILO 169 Convention, which Chile ratified in 2008. The convention establishes the right of indigenous and aboriginal communities to be consulted over matters that can affect their lands’ use.  This article reviews the convention and its implications in Peru as a precedent for Chile, followed by the first impacts of the convention in Chile and the strong opposition to energy projects. We finally review the case of El Morro and identify some implications for other Chilean mining projects. 

### Project delays due to environmental and local issues is a global problem _page 10_ 

The recent suspension of the approval of the EIS at El Morro highlights the influence that local communities can have on the development of mining projects.  In this section we review a number of projects in other regions where local protests have resulted in the delay to projects.  Such protests typically focus on the environmental implications of projects.

### ILO 169 convention and its implications in Chile 

### Introduction: The ILO 169 Convention history 

The International Labour Organization (ILO) 169 Convention, adopted in June 1989, establishes the right of indigenous and aboriginal communities to be consulted over matters that can affect their lands’ use, management and conservation, which includes mining operations.  The convention also obliges the government to take steps to foster the development of local industries and stipulates that indigenous peoples have a right to local employment, training, social security and health and education.  Countries that are members of the ILO and have ratified the convention are obliged to implement its provisions. 

The countries that have ratified the ILO 169 Convention are:  Argentina (2000), Bolivia (1991), Brazil (2002), Central African Republic (2010), Chile (2008), Colombia (1991), Costa Rica (1993), Denmark (1996), Dominica (2002), Ecuador (1998), Fiji (1998), Guatemala (1996), Honduras (1995), Mexico (1990), Nepal (2007), Netherlands (1998), Nicaragua (2010), Norway (1990), Paraguay (1993), Peru (1994), Spain (2007) and Venezuela (2002). 

The convention is a soft legislative framework, meaning that each country has to individually decide how to ensure its fulfillment.  The legal way (in countries with civil law, including the South American countries) is that the government enacts a series of laws and regulations that guarantee the rights outlined in the convention.  In general, the compliance procedure has advanced at different paces in the countries in the South American region. Argentina has not made much progress; Colombia is working on implementing the convention; Bolivia has gone beyond the requirements and most other countries have not developed much in the implementation of the convention.  Elsewhere, countries with large aboriginal populations like Canada, Australia or New Zealand, have not ratified the ILO 169 Convention.  This is because their federal governments, and not the central governments, are responsible for consulting the local populations. 

Chile ratified the convention in 2008 but has yet to enact local legislation for its compliance.  As a result, there is a lack of clarity over the rights of the miners, the government and the local communities in connection with the development of new mining projects, particularly in areas that are little developed. The legal ambivalence has already caused some problems for mining operations, as local communities are growing increasingly discontent with Chile’s lack of compliance with the convention.  For instance, construction work at the El Morro project in Region III in Chile was recently halted due to non compliance with the convention. 

Besides the degree of political will to recognize the rights of the indigenous people, another important hurdle to the implementation of the provisions of the convention is designing an appropriate legal framework.  This article will review t

he case of Peru that has already ratified and implemented the convention as it could set a precedent for Chile. 



 2012 CRU International Limited confidential 

<u>www.cruonline.crugroup.com</u> COPPER STUDIES May 2012 

3 

### Precedent for Chile: the case of Peru 

Mining regulations in Chile and Peru are fairly similar.  Both countries were successful in opening their mining industries to foreign investments in the 1990s and have since enacted a series of laws and regulations to maintain their leadership in the world. 

Peru ratified the ILO convention in 1994 and a series of laws and voluntary codes were enacted in the following years in order to implement the provisions of the convention.  For example, in mining, prior consultation with local communities was introduced as a step which had to completed as part of the Environmental Impact Study that all miners have to complete for new projects.  The local communities have to be informed and consulted 3 times about the mining project.  However, it is not mandatory to include all comments that could arise into the mining plan.  In 2003, the Ministry of Energy and Mines enacted the Supreme Decree 042-2003 that gave some guidelines on social policy matter for miners in order to improve the relationship with the neighbouring communities. 

Despite the gradual introduction of the rights of the ILO 169 Convention, local populations in Peru had been protesting and even halting the development of a number of mining projects.  The ratification of the convention by Peru may have helped spark this unrest by encouraging the indigenous peoples to claim their rights. Also, third parties, like NGOs and members of the Catholic Church, became increasingly involved in this issue. 

Local opposition has become an important obstacle to the development of new mining projects in Peru. For instance, the Conga project in Northern Peru a JV of Newmont and Buenaventura is facing serious problems due to local opposition.  There have been several instances of this in Peru and in the box below we give a few examples of mining projects that have been halted due to local opposition. 

In September 2011 the National Congress approved the _Ley de Consulta Previa a Comunidades Indigenas en el Peru_ (Prior Consultation to Indigenous Communities in Peru Law) which came into force in March/April 2012.  The law stipulates that consultation is mandatory but not legally binding, namely, miners do not have to abide by communities’ wills.  Also, the law is applied at a national level and not at a regional one. This is important as the regional authorities have no say in how the law is applied.  The Peruvian government is currently working on identifying the communities that have to be consulted and is compiling guidelines for the whole procedure.  Peru has now technically implemented the provisions of the convention but local communities are still demanding more participation. 

### ILO 169 Convention in Chile: first impacts 

Chil

e ratified the ILO 169 Convention in September 2008, and there have already been discussions about a possible framework for the implementation of the convention.  A first approach appears to be to modify the _Ley Indigena_ (Indigenous Law) of 1993 to include the consultation of such populations before undertaking investment projects.  A proposal from the government was objected to by the mining industry. 

 2012 CRU International Limited confidential 

<u>www.cruonline.crugroup.com</u> COPPER STUDIES May 2012 

4 

#### **Peru: large mining projects that did not develop due to local population opposition** 

**San Gregorio** (90s - early 2000s): Polly metallic (mainly zinc) owned by Buenaventura Group (Peru). First time in recent Peruvian history that a local community objected to a mining project due to concerns over water resources. 

**Tambogrande** (90s - early 2000s): Gold project owned by junior Manhattan Minerals (Canada). The company planned to build a pit under the town of Tambogrande.  There was poor consultation, local people protested and NGOs became involved.  The project required a relocation of the city of Tambogrande and the miner did not give enough information to the residents.  In fact, there were stories of some drillings undertaken in town streets.  A referendum in 2002 stopped the project. After Manhattan Minerals sold its mining rights, informal miners arrived to the area looking into artisanal methods to obtain gold in the area. 

**Rio Blanco** (mid-2000s): Copper project owned by Monterrico Minerals (Canada). The miner did not consult local population. It could be argued that it was not obvious who to consult given that there was no population in the immediate surroundings. Despite that, NGOs and other local groups of interest fought against the project.  Monterrico left the project and Zinjin (China) took over in 2007. Zinjin continues to work in the area. 

**Cerro Quillish** (mid-2000s): Gold project owned by the JV Newmont and Buenaventura that also owns the nearby Yanacocha mine.  The company started exploring with apparently little awareness of the importance of the mountain in the local agricultural system.  Moreover, the start of works coincided with a drought and local people concluded that the exploration works affected the eco system.  Also, the political campaign for the first regional elections took place that year and most candidates advocated the stoppage of Cerro Quillish as a key policy issue. 

**Tia Maria** (2010 – 2011): Copper project owned by Southern Peru.  The company sent confusing/early messages about their final decision regarding water policy.  They mentioned the use of underground water and of a desalination plant.  The local population, highly influenced by external agitators, voted for opposing to the project.  The project was cancelled when the EIA was rejected.  However, Southern Peru still holds the mining titles and can re-evaluate the development. 



The lack of a legal framework has

forced some projects to seek advice from a justice court on whether a population had to be consulted or not.  There are precedents of the Supreme Court ruling out environmental authorizations based on lack of fulfillment of the ILO 169 Convention.  Cases are: 

- Ecopower, a wind farm, (Chiloe – X region; 112MW): 56 wind generators with an investment of US$235M.  The location is nearby to a penguin area, close to Ancud in the island of Chiloe.  The SEA ( _Servicio de Evaluacion Ambiental_ , for its Spanish acronym) approved the EID (Environmental Impact Declaration) in August 2011.  However, the project has been facing strong opposition from 

 2012 CRU International Limited confidential 

<u>www.cruonline.crugroup.com</u> COPPER STUDIES May 2012 

5 

local communities and NGOs. Among the claims, is that there was no prior consultation with the communities of Huillinches as required by the ILO 169 Convention.  In December 2011, environmental NGOs handed in a letter to the central government explaining the environmental impact of the project and the lack of consultation to local communities.  In March 2012, the Supreme Court of Chile decided to cancel the environmental approval given that the SEA did not consult the local communities before approving the EID. 

- Exploration project Paguanta (Iquique – II region): mining exploration project, owned by Herencia Resources (AIM listed), consisting of 3 deposits and with reserves on copper, lead, silver, zinc and gold.  It is located  30km from the border with Bolivia.  Nearby mining assets include BHP Billiton’s Cerro Colorado mine and exploration projects including Codelco’s Mocha, Anglo American’s Queen Elizabeth and Codelco’s Yabricoya.  In early April 2012, the Supreme Court ordered that the miner should prepare an Environmental Impact Study (EIS) as its activities are taking place on land owned by Aymaras communities in the Huara commune.  It is understood that the SEA would have to consult the indigenous communities before giving an approval.  It is important to mention that the Paguanta project is in exploration phase for which only an EID is required.  It is hard to believe that the miner would have enough information for an EIS at this stage. 

- Regulatory Plan of San Pedro de Atacama (Calama – III region): the town of San Pedro de Atacama has a plan for its development that was designed in 1998.  However, the plan is no longer suitable because of the growing population which requires some improvements in the infrastructure (mainly to host more tourists).  So, in 2007, a new plan to expand the limits of the city began to be developed. In September 2010, the Corema (Regional Commission for the Environment) approved a new plan for the city that respected the rural landscape and maintained the condition of the nearby indigenous populations.  The community of Toconao appealed this decision to a court in Antofagasta. The community said that they were not asked their opinion despite having righ

ts according to the Chilean Constitution.  The court rejected the appeal.  The case went to the Supreme Court of Chile, which revoked the decision of the court in Antofagasta and ordered Corema to prepare an EIS and to consult the community of Toconao according to the standards of the ILO 169 Convention. 

### Strong opposition to energy projects in Chile 

Energy projects are also likely to be affected by the ILO convention.  In general, energy project have been facing stronger opposition in Chile than mining projects.  The country is short of energy and needs additional plants and transmission lines to continue growing.  For the mining industry, the sources of energy to maintain current production levels are roughly guaranteed until 2018-2020.  But, as new projects come on stream, both brownfield and greenfield, the sector will require additional power to operate. 

At the moment, there are 16,000MW of installed capacity in the country and projects under construction will add less than 3,000MW.  The copper mining industry alone consumed 3,000-3,500MW in 2011 according to our estimates and consumption can potentially grow to 6,000MW by 2021.  Other mining industries, such as gold and iron ore, are also growing in Chile and will certainly require more energy. For instance, CAP is planning to build a LNG plant to supply their operations and potentially sell energy 

 2012 CRU International Limited confidential 

<u>www.cruonline.crugroup.com</u> COPPER STUDIES May 2012 

6 

to the market.  The energy crisis could be avoided as there is a portfolio of projects that could produce, altogether, some additional 22,000MW.  Most of these projects have been halted due to opposition from local populations and some have been helped by the 169 ILO Convention. We have identified eight projects to generate energy that face strong opposition. The projects will have a total investment of US$15,835M and will produce 7,775MW. They are as follows: 

- HydroAysen (Aysen – XI region; 2,750MW): An investment of US$3,200M to produce 2.75MW. Strong opposition from the nearby population and some parts of the general public across the country. As of May 2012, the project has received the required permits to build the power plant but the ones for the transmission grid are pending. 

- Castilla (Atacama – III region; 2,350MW): Thermoelectric project, owned by Colbun (owned by Eike Batista and E.On) since 2007 that requires an investment of US$5,000M.  The owner handed in the EIS in 2008 to the Corema and, after receiving 3 reports with clarifications, corrections and/or extensions (ICSARA, for its Spanish acronym) all reflecting strong opposition from local population, it finally got approved in February 2011.  Shortly after, the opposition decided to go to court to stop the project.  A year later, a court in Antofagasta revoked the approval of the EIS. The claim was filed by the community of Totoral, where the project is located. In May 2012, the Supreme Court asked the

parties to reach a peaceful agreement but the parties’ preference is for the court to decide. The case looks unlikely to be resolved soon. 

- Punta Alcalde (Atacama – III region; 740MW): Thermoelectric project that requires an investment of US$1,400M.  The owner, Endesa, presented an EIS in February 2009 for its two generators of 370MW capacity each.  The project is planned to be located in Punta Alcalde, within the commune of Huasco.  In early May 2012, Endesa received the fourth request of an ICSARA.  Most - if not all – of the problematic issues were related to the local communities who are concerned about the environmental impacts of the project. 

- Rio Cuervo (Aysen – XI region; 640MW): An investment of US$3,600M for two hydro power generators to produce 1,100MW and a transmission line.  The project obtained the EIS approval in May 2012 after two and a half years under evaluation.  However, despite the careful analysis of the local authorities, there was still opposition to the approval of this project.  Moreover, the Supreme Court decided to invoke the EIS approval for one of the plants, just two days after the EIS approval. The company decided to halt the construction until obtaining all of the required permits. 

- Barrancones (Coquimbo – IV region; 540MW): Owned by Suez Energy, this thermoelectric project requires an investment of US$1,100M.  In October 2009, the marine authority denied the marine authorization for the project and this caused the rejection of the environmental permit.  The following year, the government asked Suez Energy to relocate the Barrancones plant, to which the company said no, referring to the fact that there was no legal base for such a request.  The company then started to search for other locations for new thermoelectric projects. 

- Termoelectricas Pacifico (Tarapaca – I region; 350MW): Project is owned by Rio Seco and requires an investment of US$750M. The company presented an EIS in 2009, which was rejected by the 

 2012 CRU International Limited confidential 

<u>www.cruonline.crugroup.com</u> COPPER STUDIES May 2012 

7 

authorities. After several corrections and amendments, the EIS was approved in May 2011. There are no indications that the project has been developed. 

- Campiche (Valparaiso – V region; 270MW): Thermoelectric project owned by AES Gener which requires an investment of US$500M. The project got an environmental approval in February 2010. A previous approval had been revoked by a court in Valparaiso due to legal problems regarding the project’s location.  Soon after the second approval was granted, the Municipality of Puchuncavi and environmentalist groups continued opposing the project.  The legal dispute went to a court in Valparaiso and then to the Supreme Court.  Construction works resumed in April 2011 but opposition from the municipality continues. The Campiche central was 89% completed as of March 2012. 

- Achibueno (Maule – VII region; 135MW): Hydroelectric project owned by E

mpresa Austral Generacion that requires an investment of US$285M. The EIS was presented for evaluation to local authorities in March 2009 and got approved in January 2011. However, the project faces strong opposition from local groups and population. The congressmen of the region are also questioning the approval of the EIS. They said that the approval was done in an unusual way and it should be reviewed. In May 2012, an organization of opponents handed in a report of analysis questioning the points of dispute of the project. In addition, there are claims to declare the area of interest and convert it into a protected one. ### First case of a major mining project halted by the 169 ILO Convention in Chile The Supreme Court of Chile upheld a February ruling by the Court of Appeals of Antofagasta to suspend the approval of the EIS for the El Morro copper-gold project. The EIS was approved by the Chilean government in March 2011, with construction intended to commence in January 2012. The decision to suspend the permit follows a filing by the Comunidad Agrнcola Los Huasco Altinos (CAHA) in May 2011, which posited that the community had not been consulted for the effects of the El Morro project as stipulated by the ILO 169 Convention. Since the ruling, construction activities have ceased at the project site, although side activities continue. The project’s owners are currently working closely with the SEA to comply with the requirements of the ILO 169 Convention. Local experts believe that it could take about 18 months to resume development work. The El Morro project is located in Region III – Atacama, near Copiapo. According to press reports, local experts say that the consultation is mandatory and it has to be done by the government as part of the EIA and the participation at that stage fulfils with the convention. In Chile, the agency that manages the environmental affairs is the SEA. It appears that an unresolved issue is who and determines which communities need to be consulted, and on what criteria. As a start, project owners give a list of affected parties while submitting the Environmental Impact Study (EIS). There is also an ongoing discussion about extending the consultation to Environmental Impact Declaration. In a similar way as in Peru, the next logical question is what communities will be consulted about and if the result is going to be binding.  2012 CRU International Limited confidential www.cruonline.crugroup.com COPPER STUDIES May 2012 8 ### III Region mining map – location of main mining assets Cerro

Copper project Copper-gold project  2012 CRU International Limited confidential www.cruonline.crugroup.com COPPER STUDIES May 2012 9 ### Some implications for the Chilean mining industry The situation at El Morro could easily emerge at other mining projects - including expansions - and energy projects. Fol

lowing the suspension of the El Morro project, the head of CAHA said that it will claim consultation for the Relincho (Teck), Pachuy (Barrick Gold) and Paso de la Flecha projects. He also said that CAHA wants to avoid the involvement of NGOs. Other large mine projects in the region are Pascua Lama (Barrick Gold), Caserones (Lumina Copper) and Cerro Casale (Barrick Gold, Kinross Gold) which could also be exposed to similar problems. For instance, Barrick Gold is undertaking a campaign to present the impacts of the Cerro Casale project. These efforts include presenting to the Chilean Congress and the company announced that they undertook two voluntary consultations to the nearby communities before handing in the EIS. Feasibility studies have been completed at the project and the project is now awaiting environmental permitting. The development of mining projects is facing several constraints, including shortages of skilled labour, technology, funding, and lack of energy supply. As mentioned above, projects to increase the energy supply in Chile are already faced with strong opposition, which in part is motivated by the ILO 169 Convention. Such opposition is contributing to the delays on the environmental permits for energy projects. Currently, an EIS for a hydro generator takes 3 – 4 years, while a copper mining project takes just 1 year. This situation hinders the development of the copper industry through delays and cost increases. And, while the ratification of the ILO 169 Convention already has had an impact on the mining industry in Chile. the full effect can only be measured once the Chilean government implements the full legislation to comply with the convention. |**Major mine**

aw aiting permitting|  2012 CRU International Limited confidential www.cruonline.crugroup.com COPPER STUDIES May 2012 10 ### Project delays due to environmental or local issues is a global problem In last month’s Copper Studies we discussed the technical challenges facing new projects. Further important factors that have led to delays are environmental and local issues, with some projects failing to get environmental permitting or being delayed due to local opposition. The revoking of the EIS

discussed above at El Morro in Chile is an example of how communities can use existing legislation (or lack of) to their advantage.  Protests by local populations are also an issue for existing operations, as evidenced by recent problems at Xstrata’s Tintaya mine in Peru.  Such protests can sometimes turn violent and will result in the temporary cessation of operations.  In this section we give some examples of projects where such issues have surfaced in recent months.  Examples can be found in all regions, showing that this is a global, not regional issue. 

Two recent examples of anti mining protests in Peru are at the existing Tintaya mine and the Minas Conga project.  A state of emergency has been called in the southern province of Espinar as the protests at Tintaya and the neighbouring Antapaccay project have turned violent.  Two people have been killed and 50 injured.  The radical protesters say that the mine causes pollution and have called for the company to increase the financial donations that it makes to the local government.  Currently 3% of pre-tax profits are given to the province of Espinar, but the protestors are calling for this to be increased to 30%, saying that the local community has not benefited from the mine.  Production is currently being phased out at the 120,000t/y Tintaya copper mine, but the 160,000t/y copper-in-concentrate Antapaccay project is set to commence in August 2012.  Such local protests are not new to Tintaya.  In May/June 2005, when the mine was owned by BHP Billiton, it was closed for nearly a month due to protests by locals complaining that the company had not invested sufficiently in the area. 

At the Minas Conga project all activity remains on hold having been suspended on 12th December due to opposition from local communities because of the environmental impact of the project.  Protests against the project flared up at the end of November with unrest spreading to the whole Cajamarca region where the mine is located.  On 4th December, the Peruvian president declared a state of emergency in certain parts of the region in order to quell the disturbances.  The protests were sparked by concern over the pressure on local water supply of the planned mining operation in a largely agricultural area, but there are additional environmental concerns.  A review of the EIS has resulted in recommendations which are now under review by the project’s owners, Newmont Mining and Buenaventura.  The project operators had been targeting a 2014/2015 start up of the project but this has now been put back to 2017. 

In Asia, the Tampakan project in the Philippines was denied environmental clearance by the Philippine Department of Environmental and Natural Resources (DENR) in January of this year.  DENR decided to hold off an issuance of environmental compliance certificate due to a ban on open pit mining imposed in 2010 by the provincial government of South Cotabato where the project is located. DENR wants the ban to be lif

ted before issuing an environmental permit. The Chamber of Mines of the Philippines (CMP) and SMI said that the decision contradicts the Philippine Constitution that stipulates that “the exploration, development and utilization of natural resources shall be under the full supervision and control of the 

 2012 CRU International Limited confidential 

<u>www.cruonline.crugroup.com</u> COPPER STUDIES May 2012 

11 

State” (as opposed to the provincial governments). They also expressed concern over the impact of this decision on investor sentiments in the Philippines. 

Environmental protestors are particularly active in the USA, and Augusta Resources’ Rosemont Ranch project in Tucson is facing strong opposition, both to the mine itself and to the associated power infrastructure.  The EIS has been approved and the company has received six of the eight permits that it requires, but the start up of construction has been delayed due to local opposition.  Protests have centred on water use, with protestors claiming that a serious fall in the level of the water table would result from the mine operations.  However, in May 2012, the Arizona Department of Environmental Quality ("ADEQ") issued the Aquifer Protection Permit ("APP"), which establishes the operating standards and controls to ensure the protection of ground water. Construction of the power line was also approved unanimously by the Arizona Corporation Commission in May 2012. 

Also in the USA, Polymet’s Northmet project has met with opposition from the local anti-mining lobby, and its EIS has been delayed several times due to revisions in order to take into account environmental concerns.  The EIS has been under preparation since 2009, when federal regulators ordered that it be revised, and is now not due for completion until 2013. 

One final case from the USA – the EPA has issued a report on the potential risks to wildlife of the Pebble project in Alaska, even before the EIS has been submitted by the development company, a joint venture between Anglo American and Northern Dynasty.  The report focuses on the impact on a large area of wetlands which is rich in wildlife and large stretches of salmon spawning streams. 

Finally, in Zambia, it was reported in March that the Ichimpe copper-cobalt project in Northern Zambia may be delayed until an environmental impact assessment report is submitted.  According to the Zambia Environmental Management Authority (ZEMA), the current plan of the mine encroaches on adjacent territories belonging to China Nonferrous Metals Co. Ltd. and therefore the development plan needs to be redesigned and approved before construction can begin.
